subject: chemistry
title: Thermal stability and flame tests
key_idea: Group 2 carbonates and nitrates decompose on heating, and become more stable down the group. A small, highly charged cation polarises the anion and weakens it. Flame colours come from excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels.

sections.heading: Thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates and nitrates

blocks.text: Heating breaks these compounds into an oxide and a gas. This section covers the products and the equations.

rows: Brown NO₂ and O₂, which relights a glowing splint

items: The oxide is a white solid.
Nitrates also give off brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide.
Carbonates and nitrates of Group 2 all decompose, but at different temperatures.
Group 2 carbonates give an oxide and carbon dioxide.
Group 2 nitrates give an oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.

blocks.text: Thermal stability **increases** down Group 2. Magnesium carbonate decomposes easily and barium carbonate needs much stronger heating.

items.meaning: How much heating a compound can take before it decomposes.
Distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.
Charge divided by size. A small ion with a high charge has a high charge density.

items: A cation with a high charge density attracts the electron cloud of a large anion and **polarises** it.
The polarised anion has a weakened bond. Heat then breaks it: CO₃²⁻ gives O²⁻ and CO₂, and NO₃⁻ gives O²⁻, NO₂ and O₂.
Down the group the cation radius increases and the charge density falls. The cation polarises the anion less.
The anion is distorted less, so more heat is needed to decompose the compound.

blocks.text: Large anions such as carbonate and nitrate are polarised easily, because their electron clouds are spread out.

items: Smaller, more highly charged cations polarise the anion more.
Down Group 2 the cations are larger, so polarisation falls and stability rises.
Carbonates and nitrates of Group 2 become harder to decompose down the group.

checks.q: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium nitrate.
Explain why barium carbonate is more thermally stable than magnesium carbonate.
checks.a: Ba²⁺ is larger than Mg²⁺, so it has a lower charge density. It polarises the carbonate ion less, so the C–O bond is weakened less and more heat is needed to decompose it.

checks.q: Describe what is seen when calcium nitrate is heated strongly, and name the gases.
checks.a: Brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide and a colourless gas, oxygen, that relights a glowing splint. A white solid, calcium oxide, remains.

blocks.text: This part covers Group 1 compounds, flame colours and the practical methods.

items: Group 1 carbonates are very stable. Only lithium carbonate decomposes in a Bunsen flame: Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂.
Lithium nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate: 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂.
Sodium to caesium nitrates give a nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
Group 1 ions have a 1+ charge and a larger radius, so they polarise the anion much less than Group 2 ions. Lithium is the smallest and polarises most.

blocks.text: The same argument applies to both groups. Group 1 compounds are more stable than Group 2 compounds in the same period.

items: Heat gives energy to electrons in the metal ion, which move to higher energy levels. They are **excited**.
The electrons fall back to lower levels and release the energy as light.
Each metal has its own energy gaps, so each gives light of its own colour.

blocks.label: Energy of the light emitted
where: ΔE: energy gap between the two levels, in J
ν: frequency of the light, in Hz

blocks.text: Two simple experiments show these patterns.

items.text: Heat a small amount of the carbonate or nitrate in a dry test tube with a Bunsen burner.
Pass the gas through limewater for CO₂. Hold a glowing splint in the tube for O₂. Look for brown fumes for NO₂.
Time how long each compound takes to give the gas. The compound that takes longest is the most stable.
Dip a clean nichrome wire in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heat it until it gives no colour. Dip it in the sample. Hold it in the edge of a blue flame and note the colour.

items: Use the same mass of each compound and the same heating, so the comparison is fair.
Concentrated hydrochloric acid cleans the wire and makes chlorides, which are volatile.

blocks.text: This part covers how to use the trend to make a prediction.

items: The size of the cation matters because the anion is large. A small cation brings its charge close to the anion and distorts it strongly.
BaCO₃ and Ba(NO₃)₂ need the highest temperatures of the Group 2 compounds. MgCO₃ and Mg(NO₃)₂ decompose at the lowest.
A cation larger than barium, such as radium, would give carbonates and nitrates that are more stable still.
